## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mūlapariyāyajātaka* (Ja 245) is a birth story belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. According to its opening frame narrative, the Buddha expounded the story while residing near Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhagavana Park, framed in connection with the "Chapter on the Succession of Causes" and serving as a backstory to the discourse on the root of all things [SuttaCentral].

The central verse of the jātaka reflects on the inexorable and destructive power of time (*kāla*) and death, opening with the theme: *Kālo ghasati bhūtāni, sabhāvena sahattanā, yo ca kālaghaso bhūto, sabhūto pācanim paci* ("Time all consumes...") [SuttaCentral; Watcharapratheep 2010]. In Buddhist discussions on the concept of death, this passage is analyzed to illustrate the dread nature of *kāla* depicted as an omnivorous and all-devouring entity consuming living beings [Watcharapratheep 2010].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any early cross-canonical parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan, nor does DharmaNexus report any internal Pali text-reuse matches with a score of 10 or higher [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral notes four translations across four modern languages [SuttaCentral].
